seo.title: Subscription Audit: Find and Cancel What You Don't Use
seo.description: A simple subscription audit: find every recurring charge, decide what to keep, cancel the rest and stop new ones from creeping back in.

h1: Subscription audit: find and cancel what you don't use
summary: A step-by-step way to list every recurring charge in your household, decide what is worth keeping, and cancel the rest without stress.
intro_html:
Subscriptions are easy to start and easy to forget. A streaming service here, extra cloud storage there, a fitness app you tried in January, a free trial that quietly turned into a paid plan. Each one feels small, so nobody looks at the total.

A subscription audit is simply sitting down once, finding every recurring charge, and asking: "Do we still use this?" It takes about an hour, it does not mean giving up the things you enjoy, and the money you free up comes back every single month. Here is how to do it, step by step.

sections.body_html:
A subscription is built to be forgotten. You agree once, and after that the money leaves your account on its own. There is no moment at the till where you hand over cash and think about it.

That is why a household can be paying for things nobody uses any more. Common examples:

  • Two or three video streaming services, when the family mostly watches one.
  • Music plans for several family members, when a shared family plan would cost less.
  • Apps bought for one project or one season, such as a language course, a photo editor or a workout app.
  • Free trials that switched to paid after a week or a month.
  • Memberships that renew once a year, so you forget they exist until the charge arrives.
  • Extra mobile data, phone insurance or add-ons from your mobile or internet provider.

A good way to see the real size is to turn everything into a yearly figure. A small monthly charge looks harmless, but twelve of them in a row can equal a week's groceries or more.

You cannot cancel what you cannot see. Set aside an hour and gather these:

  1. Bank and card statements for the last two or three months. Look for any amount that repeats on the same date.
  2. The last twelve months for yearly renewals. These are the ones people miss most often.
  3. Your phone's app store. Both major phone app stores have a "Subscriptions" page in the account settings that lists everything billed through them.
  4. Your email inbox. Search for words like "receipt", "renewal", "your plan", "trial" and "membership".
  5. Your mobile and internet bills. Some services are billed through your phone provider rather than a card.
  6. Digital wallets and payment apps, if your family uses them.

Ask everyone in the house who shares a card or account to do the same. Children and teenagers often sign up for games or apps on a parent's card.

Write it all in one list

For each item, note the name, the amount, how often it is charged (monthly or yearly), the date it renews, and who uses it. A notebook works fine, or you can add a "Subscriptions" line to your household budget calculator so you can see it next to everything else.

sections.h2: Step 2: Decide keep, cut or change
sections.body_html:
Now go through the list one line at a time. For each subscription, ask three simple questions:

  • Did anyone use it in the last month? If not, it is probably a cancel.
  • Would we sign up again today, at this price? If the honest answer is no, it has stayed out of habit.
  • Is there a free or cheaper way to get the same thing? Think of a public library card, free tiers of apps, or something you already pay for that does the same job.

Then put each item in one of three groups:

  1. Keep: used often and genuinely valued. No guilt needed.
  2. Cut: unused, forgotten or duplicated.
  3. Change: still wanted, but could cost less. For example, moving to a family or shared plan, choosing a version with adverts, dropping to a smaller storage tier, or switching from monthly to yearly billing if you are sure you will keep it all year.

Try a "rotation" for streaming

Many families keep one streaming service at a time and switch every month or two. Watch the series you wanted, cancel, then join another. You still see everything, just not all at once.

Cancelling is usually quick, but a few habits make sure it actually sticks:

  • Cancel where you signed up. If you subscribed through an app store, cancel in the app store, not by deleting the app. Deleting an app does not stop the payment.
  • Look for the cancel option in account settings, often under "Plan", "Billing" or "Membership". If you cannot find it, the help pages of the service usually explain the steps.
  • Keep proof. Take a screenshot of the confirmation page or save the confirmation email.
  • Check the next statement. Make sure the charge really stopped. If it did not, contact the company with your proof.
  • Expect a special offer. Many services offer a discount when you try to leave. It is fine to accept it if you truly want the service, but do not let it change a clear "cut" decision.

If a company keeps charging you after you have cancelled, your bank or card provider can often explain your options for disputing the payment. Rules differ from country to country, so ask them directly.

An audit works best when it is not a one-off. A few small habits keep the list short:

  • Set a reminder for every free trial. When you start one, put a reminder in your phone two days before it ends. Decide then, not after you are charged.
  • Use one card for all subscriptions. Then one statement shows you everything, and you can spot new charges quickly.
  • Give each subscription an owner. One person in the family is responsible for each service and for cancelling it when it is no longer used.
  • Repeat the audit every three to six months. The second time is much faster because your list already exists.
  • Watch for price rises. Services often raise prices with only an email notice. When one arrives, ask the three questions again.

Where to put the money you save

Money from cancelled subscriptions disappears just as quietly as it was spent, unless you give it a job. As soon as you cancel, consider moving the same amount each month into savings, an emergency fund, or extra payments on debt. That way the saving is real, not just on paper.

Here is how an audit might look for one family. The amounts are only an illustration, so think of them in your own currency.

  • Three video streaming services: they mostly watch one. They keep one and rotate the others.
  • Two separate music plans: they switch to one shared family plan.
  • A workout app nobody has opened since spring: cancelled.
  • Extra cloud storage on two phones: they move photos to one shared plan and cancel the second.
  • A yearly magazine subscription renewing next month: they set a reminder and decide they still read it, so it stays.

Nothing they actually enjoy is gone. Yet several monthly charges have disappeared, and the yearly total of what they saved is often bigger than people expect. Write the new, lower subscriptions figure into your budget so you can see the difference in your monthly plan.

faq.q: How often should I do a subscription audit?
faq.a: Once every three to six months works well for most households. It is also worth a quick check whenever you get a price-rise email or start a new free trial.

faq.q: Does deleting an app cancel the subscription?
faq.a: No. Deleting an app usually does not stop the payment. Cancel inside your account settings or in your phone's app store subscriptions page, and keep the confirmation.

faq.q: Is it better to pay yearly or monthly?
faq.a: Yearly plans are often cheaper per month, but only if you are sure you will use the service all year. If you are unsure, monthly billing makes it easier to stop when you no longer need it.

faq.q: What if I can't find where a charge comes from?
faq.a: Search your email for the name shown on your statement, and check your phone's app store and your mobile bill. If you still cannot identify it, contact your bank or card provider and ask them about it.
